name: Naïve Cynicism
description: People can overestimate how biased, strategic, or self-interested other people's judgments are. Suspicion itself becomes biased, so disagreement gets read as ulterior motive faster than reality warrants.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to cross-functional disputes, research readouts, moderation/fairness debates, and stakeholder conflict: teams can assume opponents are reasoning in bad faith while seeing their own interpretation as comparatively clean.
prevalence_note: A real named social-psychology construct, but the explicit label is uncommon in everyday product/UX vocabulary compared with adjacent ideas like naïve realism, bias blind spot, or false consensus.

findings.description: Across several lab and field studies, participants expected other people's responsibility judgments—but not their own—to be motivationally biased, and in competitive settings they expected teammates to be less biased than opponents, establishing the core pattern Kruger and Gilovich called naïve cynicism.
findings.source_title: "Naive cynicism" in everyday theories of responsibility assessment: On biased assumptions of bias.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
